title: Khene (Lao bamboo mouth organ)
summary: The khene is the bamboo mouth organ of Laos: two rows of paired reed pipes set in a small wooden wind chest. The player breathes in and out through the same mouthpiece while fingers cover or lift small holes, so the sound never has to stop for a breath.
howToPlay: Each coloured mark falls toward a pipe; when it reaches the line, press that pipe's hole and the pipe sounds.
Hold the longer notes for as long as their tail lasts, then move to the next pipe on time.
Two low drone pipes hum under the tune the whole time, as they do on a real khene. Learn the slow figure first.
rules: Ten pipes are laid out over two octaves of a five-note mode (A, C, D, E, G); longer pipes sound lower.
Two low drone pipes sound from the first breath to the last note; they are not scored.
Each figure is played twice, in four beats to the bar, after a one-bar count-in.
A note on the beat scores in full, a close one scores less, and an extra stroke costs a little.
The round ends when the last note is judged; stars follow the percentage of the full score.
Sustained notes are judged by their start; the tail shows how long the sound lasts.
heritageNote: The khene has been played in Laos and across the Lao-speaking lands of north-east Thailand for centuries, as a solo voice and as the partner of sung poetry in village shows. Makers cut the bamboo pipes, set a brass or silver reed in each and fix the pitch with beeswax; the instrument is passed from player to player by ear.
